Choosing a method
Formulas
References for fieldwork
Understand measurements, volume table families and their applicability before interpreting a result.
These documents explain principles. They certify neither GeoSylva\'s calculations, nor a local volume table, nor a payable quantity.
Forest inventory
CNPF · e-for-OWN · June 2019 · PDF pp. 11–12
Diameter measurement reference, diameter classes and heights of sample trees. The height of a representative tree does not become an individual measurement for every tree in its class.
Standing timber volume estimation
CRPF Île-de-France / Centre · December 2013 · pp. 1–4

Distinguish height to a specified cut-off, mid-point diameter and diameter at 1.30 m; match the estimate to stem form. Commercial conventions and their current applicability still need checking for the relevant contract.
Even-aged stands and slenderness
CNPF · e-for-OWN · June 2019 · PDF p. 6
Examples of the height/diameter ratio in the context of first thinnings. Their interpretation depends on the stand; they do not establish a universal stability threshold.
Rapid and slow volume tables
Léon Schaeffer · Revue forestière française · 1949 · pp. 7–13
The publication describes two single-entry families. “Rapid” and “slow” do not mean “one” and “two” entries. Choosing a table number requires suitable calibration.
Log measurement
FAO · K. Jayaraman · Statistical Manual for Forestry Research · § 6.2.1

Huber, Smalian and Newton formulas according to available sections and their positions. The manual distinguishes these measurements from prediction equations requiring calibration to a species and stand. Document in English.
Basal area and quadratic mean diameter
Australian National University · Brack and Wood · Stand basal area
Definitions of individual tree section area, their sum and quadratic mean diameter. Preserve units and the measured population when converting to a per-hectare value. Document in English.
Read the source document

Start with the available measurements
A table name or location alone is insufficient to choose a reliable equation.
Single-entry volume table
One dimension · usually diameter or circumference

The equation estimates volume from one dimension with a defined measurement reference. It may require a table number calibrated to the stand. Not requiring height does not remove the need to check applicability to the observed timber.
Double-entry volume table
Two dimensions · usually diameter and height

The method defines the required height: total, to a specified cut-off, or another reference. Stand dominant height or a diameter class mean height cannot replace an individual height without an explicit estimation model.
Check the domain of applicability

Species or species group, size range, stem form, stand structure and site conditions: check what the method covers. Use the location of the parcel or survey; the phone\'s current GPS position or a downloaded pack does not establish that a volume table applies.
Describe each measurement

Distinguish measured diameter from class midpoint, total height from commercial height, measurement from estimate, and individual from collective reference. For individual H/D, height and diameter must refer to the same tree. Unknown values remain unknown.
Keep the references
Keep the method and version, coefficient source, measurement date, protocol, cut-off and bark convention. A new table or correction must not reinterpret results from an already closed survey.
No universal accuracy is guaranteed. An error estimate or uncertainty interval requires documented validation under the method\'s conditions of use.
Clearly defined quantities
These identities explain units and required data. Their presence in this guide does not activate a calculation or extrapolation in your records.
Basal area of a tree
D in cm; g in m². Circular section at the diameter measurement level. For observed trees, G is the sum of g. A count by diameter class gives an approximation tied to that class\'s reference diameter.
Quadratic mean diameter
G in m², N a strictly positive tree count, Dg in cm. G and N must describe exactly the same population. Dg uses squared diameters, not their arithmetic mean.
Per-hectare conversion

A is the actually inventoried horizontal area in m², strictly positive. This ratio assumes a complete count of the chosen population over that area. Sampling requires its own weights; a cadastral boundary alone is insufficient.
Individual slenderness H/D

H is total height in m and D is diameter in cm for the same individual tree, with an explicit measurement convention. The ratio is dimensionless. Commercial height, class height or a collective mean diameter cannot yield this individual H/D.
H/D describes a proportion. Its value alone does not predict stability: species, stand structure, rooting, exposure and interventions also need assessment. No universal threshold is applied here.
Geometric log volumes
Huber: V = L × Sm\nSmalian: V = L × (S0 + S1) / 2\nNewton: V = L × (S0 + 4Sm + S1) / 6

L in m; section areas S0 at the start, Sm at mid-length and S1 at the end in m²; V in m³. For a circular section, S = π × (d / 200)² with d in cm. Measure at the required positions and preserve the over-bark or under-bark convention.

These geometric formulas apply to measured logs; they are not standing-tree volume tables. A provisional volume does not become a payable quantity without the applicable convention and commercial validation. A stack envelope includes voids and does not directly give solid wood volume.
